headings.title: Introduction and Pathophysiology of Leprosy
headings.content: Leprosy, also known as Hansen's disease, is a chronic infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae, an acid-fast, rod-shaped bacillus that primarily targets the peripheral nerves and skin. Understanding the pathophysiology of leprosy is vital for nursing students because the bacterium has a strong predilection for cooler areas of the body, such as the skin, upper respiratory tract, superficial nerves, eyes, and testes. Transmission is widely believed to occur primarily through droplets from the nose and mouth during close and frequent contact with untreated cases. Once inside the host, M. leprae invades Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system, leading to demyelination, nerve damage, and subsequent loss of sensation. The clinical manifestations of the disease are largely determined by the patient's cell-mediated immune response. In individuals with a robust immune response, the proliferation of the bacteria is contained, whereas those with a poor cell-mediated immunity experience widespread bacterial multiplication and tissue infiltration. As nursing professionals in Nigeria and globally, recognizing these early pathological changes is essential for timely intervention, preventing irreversible nerve damage, and breaking the chain of transmission within vulnerable communities through active case finding and contact tracing.

headings.title: Classification and Clinical Manifestations
headings.content: Leprosy is clinically classified using the Ridley-Jopling system, which categorizes the disease based on the patient's immunological response into tuberculoid (TT), borderline tuberculoid (BT), mid-borderline (BB), borderline lepromatous (BL), and lepromatous (LL) forms. For practical field management, the World Health Organization (WHO) simplifies this into Paucibacillary (PB) and Multibacillary (MB) leprosy. Paucibacillary leprosy typically involves five or fewer skin lesions with no bacteria found in skin smears, representing a high cell-mediated immune response. In contrast, Multibacillary leprosy features more than five lesions, often with widespread distribution, symmetrical skin infiltration, nodules, and positive skin smears due to low cell-mediated immunity. Clinical manifestations vary widely; tuberculoid leprosy presents with well-demarcated, anesthetic hypopigmented or reddish skin patches accompanied by nerve enlargement. Lepromatous leprosy presents with generalized skin thickening, leonine facies, loss of eyebrows and eyelashes, and symmetric peripheral sensory loss known as 'stocking-glove' anesthesia. Nurses must be adept at differentiating these presentations, as accurate classification dictates the specific duration and combination of pharmacological therapy required for successful patient outcomes.

headings.title: Diagnostic Evaluation and Clinical Assessment
headings.content: Diagnostic evaluation of leprosy relies heavily on a thorough clinical assessment combined with physical examinations and laboratory tests. Nurses play a crucial role in identifying cardinal signs, which include hypo-pigmented or reddish skin patches with definite loss of sensation, thickened or enlarged peripheral nerves (such as the ulnar, greater auricular, or peroneal nerves), and the presence of acid-fast bacilli on skin slit smears. Sensory testing is a cornerstone of the clinical assessment; nurses use tools like Semmes-Weinstein monofilaments or simple cotton wisps, pinpricks, and warm/cold test tubes to evaluate touch, pain, and temperature sensation in suspicious patches and along nerve pathways. Slit-skin smears, taken from earlobes and lesions, are examined under a microscope using Ziehl-Neelsen staining to detect M. leprae. In settings where specialized tests are available, skin biopsies may be performed to confirm histological features. A comprehensive neurological assessment is also mandatory to document baseline nerve function impairment, which guides treatment efficacy and helps monitor for potential complications or reactions throughout the course of therapeutic management.

headings.title: Pharmacological Management and Multidrug Therapy
headings.content: Pharmacological management of leprosy has been revolutionized by Multidrug Therapy (MDT), recommended by the World Health Organization since the early 1980s to prevent drug resistance associated with monotherapy. MDT combines potent anti-leprosy drugs: rifampicin, dapsone, and clofazimine. The treatment regimen is strictly divided based on the WHO classification. For Paucibacillary (PB) leprosy, adults receive supervised monthly doses of rifampicin along with daily self-administered dapsone for a duration of six months. For Multibacillary (MB) leprosy, the regimen includes monthly supervised doses of rifampicin and clofazimine, supplemented by daily self-administered dapsone and clofazimine for a duration of 12 to 24 months, or until skin smears are clear. Nurses bear significant responsibility in drug administration, monitoring patient compliance, educating patients about potential side effects—such as the reddish-brown skin discoloration caused by clofazimine—and ensuring regular follow-up visits. Direct Observation Therapy (DOT) for monthly doses ensures high adherence rates and minimizes the emergence of drug-resistant strains of M. leprae within the community.

headings.title: Nursing Care and Prevention of Disabilities
headings.content: Nursing care for patients with leprosy extends far beyond pharmacological administration; it encompasses holistic management focused on the prevention of disabilities (POD) and self-care training. Because nerve damage results in anesthesia and muscle weakness (such as claw hand, foot drop, and lagophthalmos), patients are at high risk for secondary injuries, burns, and chronic ulcers without realizing it. Nurses must educate patients on daily self-care routines, including inspecting their hands and feet daily using a mirror for cuts, blisters, or swelling. Patients should be taught to soak, scrub, and oil dry skin to prevent fissures, wear well-fitting protective footwear to avoid plantar ulcerations, and use gloves when handling hot objects to prevent thermal burns. For patients with lagophthalmos (inability to close the eyes fully), regular use of protective eyewear and lubricating eye drops is essential to prevent corneal ulceration and blindness. Documenting nerve function, teaching joint range-of-motion exercises, and providing psychological support are all vital nursing interventions that preserve functional independence and enhance the overall quality of life for affected individuals.

headings.title: Complications and Reactional States
headings.content: Complications in leprosy often manifest as acute reactional states, which are immunological episodes that can occur before, during, or after MDT and can rapidly cause severe nerve damage. There are two primary types of reactions: Type 1 (Reversal Reaction) and Type 2 (Erythema Nodosum Leprosum or ENL). Type 1 reactions are delayed-type hypersensitivity reactions common in borderline forms, characterized by sudden inflammation of existing skin lesions, edema, and acute neuritis with severe nerve pain and tenderness. Type 2 reactions are immune-complex mediated, typically occurring in lepromatous leprosy, and present with painful subcutaneous red nodules, fever, malaise, iridocyclitis, and orchitis. Nurses must identify these reactional states immediately because emergency management with corticosteroids (such as prednisolone) or thalidomide is often required to halt acute nerve function deterioration and prevent permanent paralysis or blindness. Close monitoring of nerve function, patient reporting of sudden pain or weakness, and adherence to anti-inflammatory regimens are core nursing responsibilities during these critical flare-ups.

headings.title: Patient Education, Rehabilitation, and Stigma Reduction
headings.content: Patient education, rehabilitation, and stigma reduction are fundamental pillars in comprehensive leprosy care. Due to centuries of historical myths and misconceptions, leprosy is frequently associated with severe social stigma, ostracization, and psychological distress, which can deter individuals from seeking early medical treatment. Nurses play a frontline advocacy and educational role by dispelling myths, reassuring patients and their families that leprosy is fully curable with MDT, and emphasizing that patients on treatment are no longer infectious. Counseling helps patients cope with the emotional impact of diagnosis and potential deformities. Furthermore, community-based rehabilitation programs focus on vocational training, physical therapy, and reconstructive surgery referrals, enabling patients to regain economic self-sufficiency and reintegrate successfully into society. By fostering a compassionate, stigma-free healthcare environment, nurses empower patients to complete their treatment regimens, embrace self-care practices, and live productive, dignified lives within their communities.
